turn1.content: I am planning a small vegetable garden behind my house in a region with hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters. The plot is about six metres long and three metres wide, it gets direct sun from late morning until early evening, and the soil is heavy clay that cracks when it dries out in July. Last year I tried tomatoes, courgettes and green beans directly in the ground without preparing anything: the tomatoes split, the courgettes were fine for a month and then got a white powder on the leaves, and the beans never really climbed. I can spend a few weekends on preparation, I would rather not use chemical fertilisers, and I have access to horse manure from a neighbour and to a lot of fallen leaves in autumn. What should I do to the soil first, which crops are realistic for a beginner here, and how should I organise watering so I do not waste water during the summer?
Start with the soil: work in well-rotted manure and shredded leaves in autumn, mulch heavily, and water deeply but rarely with drip lines.

turn2.content: Thank you, that helps. Two follow-up questions. First, the manure my neighbour offers is fresh, from this month: can I put it on the beds now if I only plant in spring, or will it burn the roots, and how long should it compost first? Second, about the drip lines: I have an outdoor tap with normal pressure and no electricity near the garden. Is a simple timer on the tap with a pressure reducer enough, how many litres per week would a tomato plant need in July in my climate, and should I water in the morning or in the evening to limit the powdery leaves I saw on the courgettes?
